title: Add initial support for BBLog files

notes.body: Presumably you mean `"frame.bblocks.serno"` or something such as that.

No, I am referring to a field Serial Number, which is part of Black Block Log (bblog), listed under frames.

BBLog information can show up as an individual block, then it is dissected by the handler in packet-bblog.c. Then it describes an internal event in the TCP stack of FreeBSD. But this information can also show up in addition to a send/received packet. Then I'm showing this information in the frame section.

Presumably, you do not mean `"frame.bblog.ticks"`, as there's already a `"frame.bblog.ticks"` frame, but instead mean something such as `"frame.bblog.serno"` rather than `"frame.bblog.ticks"` for the "Serial Number" field.

Yes, you are absolutely right. Fixed.

Do you mean "BBLog files" or "Netflix Black Box Log custom pcapng blocks"?

And have Netflix documented those blocks?

Well, this is the story:
* Netflix developed the TCP black box feature and use custom blocks using their PEN.
* Then this feature was upstreamed to FreeBSD. But it still uses the Netflix PEN.
* So the file format is documented in the way that you can get the daemon writing these files from the FreeBSD ports collection. The format has a version field. I plan to keep it in sync with the FreeBSD sources.
Does this answer your question?

added 1 commit
  • 759ae57b - Add initial support for BBLog files
[Compare with previous version](/wireshark/wireshark/-/merge_requests/3990/diffs?diff_id=236144133&start_sha=a31875a311c9fb24314b47bd35e7e8a7c6a980a0)

> So the file format is documented in the way that you can get the daemon writing these files from the FreeBSD ports collection.

From what I see in the changes, the bulk of the file format is documented [here](https://pcapng.github.io/pcapng/draft-tuexen-opsawg-pcapng.html) - [here](https://pcapng.github.io/pcapng/draft-tuexen-opsawg-pcapng.html#name-custom-options) and [here](https://pcapng.github.io/pcapng/draft-tuexen-opsawg-pcapng.html#name-custom-block), in particular.

The part that's *not* documented is the syntax and semantics of the blocks and options in question; is that documented anywhere other than code in FreeBSD and in its ports collection?

No, it is not. There is another C based program which can be used to read the BBLog files, but that is very developer oriented. That is one of the reasons I decided to implement use much more user friendly reader in Wireshark. It will evolve over time, but I wanted to get the infrastructure in. This is stable. The C structures I use are basically extracted from the FreeBSD header files, since I can't use them on all platforms.

I tested the dumper code and the Wireshark reader side on 64-bit platforms with little endian and big endian support. So I assume the infrastructure code is stable.

What will evolve is the display of the fields for various events. But most of this will happen in packet-bbr.c.

Do you require packet formats using a PEN to be defined publically in some way?
resolved all threads

> No, it is not.

"It" presumably meaning "the pcapng custom block and options that they added", and "not" presumably meaning "not documented".

> There is another C based program which can be used to read the BBLog files,

A "BBLog file" is a pcapng file that happens to contain those blocks or options, so that's presumably a program that reads pcapng or some subset thereof, and supports the custom block and options in question.

> Do you require packet formats using a PEN to be defined publically in some way?

It would be preferable if any code in wireshark to handle particular custom blocks could point to *something* that indicated the format - a document would be ideal (yo, Reed!), but a header file and code would be second-best.  That makes maintenance easier, as there's something against which to check Wireshark's dissection.

What I meant is that the data contained in the custom blocks or custom options using the Netflix PEN are documented right now by only having the code available in the FreeBSD ports tree of the program which writes these files.

If these custom blocks or custom options contain structures, these structures are available in a header of the FreeBSD source tree: [tcp_log_buf.h](https://cgit.freebsd.org/src/tree/sys/netinet/tcp_log_buf.h).

You are correct, with BBLog file I mean any file which contains the particular custom blocks and custom options. In reality, these files are the ones written by [tcplog_dumper](https://cgit.freebsd.org/ports/tree/net/tcplog_dumper).

I agree, that it would be preferable to have a well written specification. However, that is not the case. But we have source code to look at...

If you are wondering if BBLog files are used at all: they are heavily used within Netflix and I hope with making these readable via Wireshark they can also be used by the FreeBSD community to improve the TCP stacks and help debugging problems users are reporting.

So is this acceptable?

Is there some reason not to use `REC_TYPE_CUSTOM_BLOCK` for the BBLog blocks, given that they're pcapng custom blocks?
Hmm. One can do that and do a switch case. Would you prefer that?

Right now the generic unknown custom blocks are handled separately from known custom blocks. But if you prefer, I can merge them. Some structs would then be integrated by using unions. Just let me know and I change it.
I would prefer to have as much common processing as possible for custom blocks and options.
OK, I change it. There will be not less or more code. Just some more selectors in accessing fields (combining two structures in one using a union).
No `REC_TYPE_CUSTOM_BLOCK` anymore...
So are the fields in the custom option always little-endian, regardless of the byte order of the host that wrote the file?

The fields in the NFLX custom options and NFLX custom blocks are always little endian. The only exception is addresses and port numbers, there are always in host byte order.
Since a node can read and write custom options and custom blocks without knowing its structure, these fields must have a fixed byte order. I think this is even written down in the pcapng spec...

> The fields in the NFLX custom options and NFLX custom blocks are always little endian.

"fields in the NFLX custom blocks" presumably means "the fields in the Custom Data field", as...

> I think this is even written down in the pcapng spec...

...the pcapng spec says

> Private Enterprise Number (32 bits): An IANA-assigned Private Enterprise Number identifying the organization which defined the Custom Block. See Section 6.1 for details. The PEN MUST be encoded using the same endianness as the Section Header Block it is within the scope of.

so if, in a section where the SHB is big-endian, the PEN is little-endian, that's not a valid pcapng file.

To be precise:
* For custom options the Block Type, Block Total Length and PEN are written in the byte order indicated in the SHB.
* For custom options contained in the SHB and the EPB, the Custom Option Code, Custom Option Length, and PEN are written in the byte order indicated in the SHB.
* For custom options in custom blocks the Custom Option Code, Custom Option Length, and PEN are written in litte endian.

Isn't that OK?

> For custom options in custom blocks the Custom Option Code, Custom Option Length, and PEN are written in litte endian.

Where does it say that in the pcapng spec?

Is the idea here to permit programs that don't know about BBLog custom blocks to blindly copy the block without having to know where the custom data ends and the options begin?

> Where does it say that in the pcapng spec?

Nowhere. The format of the custom block does not allow a reader of the pcapng file not knowing the format of the Custom Data detect any options.

> Is the idea here to permit programs that don't know about BBLog custom blocks to blindly copy the block without having to know where the custom data ends and the options begin?

Yes. This is my understanding of custom options which can be copied. I implemented the support of customs options in wireshark that way and tested:
* Generating a BBLog file on a big endian host.
* Reading this file on a litte endian host and writing it out in litte endian format.
Then the BBLog file should still be readable on litte endian and big endian systems. Or am I missing something?

> This is my understanding of custom options which can be copied.

Then [section 6.4 "Endianness Issues" of the pcapng spec](https://pcapng.github.io/pcapng/draft-tuexen-opsawg-pcapng.html#name-endianness-issues) should be expanded so that

> Therefore, the vendor should either encode all of their fields in a consistent manner, such as always in big-endian or always little-endian format, regardless of the host platform's endianness, or should encode some flag in the Custom Data payload to indicate in which endianness the rest of the payload is written.

notes that, in the Options section of a Custom Block, the option type, length, and data must also be encoded in a consistent manner.
I agree. But that is an issue with the specification, not with this code.

> But that is an issue with the specification, not with this code.

I updated the spec.  Ideally, this should have been recognized at the time the Custom Blocks were defined or, if not, at the time the first Custom Block containing options was created, but so it goes.
Thanks for updating the specification. Well, at least it was recognised the first time we added support custom blocks using options in wireshark...

> > * or custom options in custom blocks the Custom Option Code, Custom Option Length, and PEN are written in litte endian.
> 
> Isn't that OK?

Not for the PEN it isn't - not even one little bit.

As of 2015(!), the pcapng spec said:

> Private Enterprise Number: An IANA-assigned Private Enterprise Number identifying the organization which defined the Custom Option.  See Supported Use-Cases for details.  The PEN number MUST be encoded using the same endianess as the Section Header Block it is within the scope of.

and

> Private Enterprise Number: An IANA-assigned Private Enterprise Number identifying the organization which defined the Custom Block.  See Supported Use-Cases for details.  The PEN number MUST be encoded using the same endianess as the Section Header Block it is within the scope of.

so if Netflix decided to make it universally little-endian, they failed to read the spec closely enough.

There is no reason to forcibly encode it as little-endian as, unlike the contents of the block or option, the header of the block or option, including the PEN, is defined by the pcapng spec, and thus even software that is ignorant of the format Custom Data in the block or option, and therefore can only blindly copy that data over when writing it, knows enough to write out the PEN in the correct byte order.

Writing out the PEN in big-endian order in a little-endian section, or in little-endian order in a big-endian section, will cause software that follows the pcapng spec to be unable to recognize Netflix custom blocks or options.

Fortunately, if any programs actually *have* written invalid big-endian pcapng files with the PEN for Netflix custom blocks or options as 0xC6 0x2A 0x00 0x00 rather than as 0x00 0x00 0x2A 0xC6, then programs that follow the spec will see the PEN as 3324641280 and, as of today, [the highest assigned PEN value is 57891](https://www.iana.org/assignments/enterprise-numbers/enterprise-numbers), and there are 3324583389 left to assign before 3324641280 is assigned to anyone.  If  an average of 10000 PENs are assigned per day, we won't get there for another 900 years or so.

I.e., readers can, if necessary, check for 3324641280 as well as 10949, and that hack will probably last a few centuries; if we ever reach the point that 3324641280 is assigned, the chances are probably slim that anybody will care about those old captures, especially if all software that writes out Netflix custom blocks and options, and that is likely ever to be run on a big-endian machine (meaning "old desktop machines like PowerPC Macs, SPARC machines, big-endian PowerPC/Power ISA machines/LPARs, System/390 and z/Architecture machines, and some MIPS machines"), is fixed as soon as possible.

> There is no reason to forcibly encode it as little-endian as, unlike the contents of the >  > block or option, the header of the block or option, including the PEN, is defined by the > > pcapng spec, and thus even software that is ignorant of the format Custom Data in the block > or option, and therefore can only blindly copy that data over when writing it, knows enough > to write out the PEN in the correct byte order.

I'm only referring to those custom options which are contained in the custom block. How can a reader distinguish how many bytes are `Custom Data` and how many bytes are `Options`? I don't see this. This is a limitation of the specification of custom blocks, I think.

Since a reader not knowing the specific structure of a particular common block, it can't change the byte ordering of any fields in it.

The specification says in Section 6.4:
```
Therefore, the vendor should either encode all of their fields in a consistent manner,
such as always in big-endian or always little-endian format, regardless of the host
platform's endianness, or should encode some flag in the Custom Data payload to
indicate in which endianness the rest of the payload is written.
```

Therefore I decided to go a little endian...

What am I missing?
